title: `tailscale up` indefinitely hangs on Debian Bookworm, Tailscale version 1.62.1
body:
### What is the issue?

`tailscale up` indefinitely hangs on Debian Bookworm, Tailscale version 1.62.1.
I expect `tailscale up` to work like normal.

`journalctl -u tailscaled.service` and `systemctl status tailscaled` log output:
```
Apr 03 11:28:08 shitbook tailscaled[1906]: control: LoginInteractive -> regen=true
Apr 03 11:28:08 shitbook tailscaled[1906]: control: doLogin(regen=true, hasUrl=false)
Apr 03 11:28:13 shitbook tailscaled[1906]: Received error: fetch control key: Get "https://<redacted-host>/key?v=88": context deadline exceeded
```

Ignore my hostname, I'm actually running this on a Chromebook (shouldn't be the problem as it worked before).

### Steps to reproduce

1. Run the install script
2. Run `sudo tailscale up`
3. Hangs infinitely until I press `ctrl`+`c`. The output given when pressing `ctrl`+`c` is `context canceled`.

### Are there any recent changes that introduced the issue?

I have no idea. I do know that I'm installing on a fresh machine. Tailscale worked fine on the previous install. I had never updated the package so this could be why I'm experiencing this now.
`sudo tailscale login` also hangs indefinitely. I had removed my last install's machine removed from the admin panel, and since I'm not logged in, that wouldn't help anyways.

### OS

Linux

### OS version

Debian Bullseye

### Tailscale version

1.62.1

### Other software

I do not have any extra software.

### Bug report

BUG-70f373e33198105f37a0c5547e166ee0d4ea0ee480add064d13a7af56f428398-20240403162538Z-c3cf4b4356b6ca23

comments.author: reporter
comments.body:
It also appears that my `/etc/resolv.conf` is not complete. I actually have my old `/etc/resolv.conf` (from the previous install) and the 2 look similar but the current one is missing some things.

Old `resolv.conf`:
```
# resolv.conf(5) file generated by tailscale
# For more info, see https://tailscale.com/s/resolvconf-overwrite
# DO NOT EDIT THIS FILE BY HAND -- CHANGES WILL BE OVERWRITTEN

nameserver 100.100.100.100
search (redacted).ts.net lxd
```

Current `resolv.conf`:
```
domain lxd
search lxd
nameserver 100.115.92.193
```
Before I sent this comment, I tried overriding my current `resolv.conf` to my old `resolv.conf` and after a reboot and running `sudo tailscale up`, it changes back to the current output. Any ideas?

comments.author: participant1
comments.body:
Here's how I solved my issue.

I am using Netplan.  I had different name server entries on my internal and external interfaces.  I edited /etc/netplan/netplan.yaml to remove the nameservers and search domain from my LAN interface.  I appended the name servers and the seaarch domain to my WAN interface.

run: netplan apply

It may not be everyone's solution, yet it did work in my instance.  In my case I have 2 nics and a public interface because it's a jumpbox.

This is a regression as it worked in the past.

comments.author: participant3
comments.body:
It happened to me yesterday while I was setting up my resolv.conf. Its been awhile since my docker containers cannot resolve DNS. Im using Pi-hole as my DNS resolver. Hosted on the same Debian. 

Since I couldnt figure it out, I decided to reset my resolv.conf on Debian by running "sudo apt-get remove --purge resolvconf && sudo apt-get install resolvconf" . and that worked, after putting 127.0.0.1 as the nameserver in resolv.conf, everything was working. The host and dockers containers can resolve DNS .

But somewhat in the process Tailscale failed. I thought it had something to do with me messing with resolv.conf but everything can resolve DNS on host and docker containers with no issues. Ping <redacted-host> as well, no issue. So I am at a dead end how to fix this issue. I am sure like you said related to nameservers. Just I am not sure where to look.

"Received error: fetch control key: Get "https://<redacted-host>/key?v=88": context deadline exceeded"

comments.author: participant2
comments.body: Being able to ping/resolve a host is not the same as being able to connect to the specific port/service, eg. HTTPS. I'm also able to ping the controlplane, but the https port is filtered.

comments.body: Ok, that makes sense.

I also have another Tailscale in a docker container for an exit node for commercial VPN and connects perfectly. I did tried disable the Tailscale in Docker just for good measure, still no luck. It won't connect on the host Debian itself, so I am started to wondering if Tailscale uses other than resolv.conf.

comments.author: participant4
comments.body:
@reporter Hi, I encountered the same issue. After updating Tailscale using "sudo apt-get update", the Tailscale connection was lost. It seems that this issue originates from an authorization problem, where the authorization page is blocked by network administration. Here's a potential solution:

1. Switch your server's internet connection to another ungoverned network, such as a personal hotspot.
2. Start your Tailscale service using this personal connection.
3. Then, switch your connection back to the original governed network.

comments.author: participant9
comments.body:
I'm not an expert, but your logs says that the server is continually rejecting the connection to get the key from the controlplane. 
My theory is that some new changes in some managed networks is interfering with the authentication process of the controlplane. So the only way to troubleshoot it locally is contacting someone with administrative access to the managed network to follow the authentication process to find where if failing exactly to pinpoint the cause of the problem.
As I'm aware the only one that have solved it by identifiying the exact rule in the managed network that caused the problem is @participant13 in #12038

comments.author: participant9
comments.body:
The easiest way to test if the problem is your home network or your ISP, is connecting to another network of that uses the same ISP, for example a neighbor and check if tailscale works. If it works in the other network it means that the problem originated from your home network configuration, if it not, it means that the problem is the ISP.
Another way is to check if you really are in total control of your home network router or if your ISP gave you a limited access, the easiest way is by activating ICMP in your router and check if you can ping the public IP of your router from your cellphone or any other device that's is not in the same subnet as your router. This method don't always works as it depends if the ISP follows the standard of blocking the inbound ICMP traffic by default.
